title: Larne & Kilwaughter
standfirst: East Antrim records preserve several Glasgow households from 1653 onward. One later father-and-son link is explicit; the connections between the older households, and to collateral Irish lines, are still questions.
question: Can the seventeenth-century Larne, Glenarm and Kilwaughter occurrences be connected to the later documented Kilwaughter family without filling the missing generations by name or locality alone?
answer: The 20 December 1764 Ballykeel lease proves that James Glasgow was Robert Glasgow’s son. It does not name Robert’s father, connect him to the 1653 or 1669 householders, or establish a Scottish origin. Later Larne and Inishrush comparisons are useful hypotheses, not a joined pedigree.

chapters.title: Separate early occurrences
body: A 1653 deposition places Robert Glaskow at Larne. The 1669 hearth-money roll records Elizabeth at Glenarm and James and John at Kilwaughter.
These are documented local occurrences, not a proved founding family or a line of descent.

chapters.title: Larne property, but not kinship
body: A 1736 Newtown lease names William and Hugh Glasgow as joint lessees, and a 1757 deed independently refers to their head lease. Neither document states that they were related.
The 1749 mortgage and later assignments add business and occupational occurrences, not parentage.

chapters.title: A documented Kilwaughter father and son
body: The register chronology and later equity material reconstruct Robert Glasgow and Rachel Wilson’s household at Kilwaughter. The 1738 lease associates Robert, Rachel and James junior, but does not call James a son.
The original 1764 Ballykeel lease does: its continuation calls him “Jas Glasgow son of the sd Robt”.

chapters.title: A family continues to South Carolina
body: James Glasgow’s 1775 will and the later equity case support James and Mary Crosier’s South Carolina household and name Archibald among their children.
That American continuation does not supply Robert’s parentage in Ireland or join the family to the older Larne occurrences.

chapters.title: A later estate question
body: The Larne monument explicitly names James Glasgow as a son of elder Hugh. The 1843 marriage settlement names property of a deceased Hugh Glasgow, but does not call that Hugh Mary’s father.
The current James–Hugh–Mary chain is a low-confidence working hypothesis. Mary may instead be William’s monument-recorded daughter, whose 1844 death conflicts with the candidate 1843 death.

chapters.title: Mill auction in Larne, Kilwaughter and Inver
body: A 10 September 1804 Caledonian Mercury advertisement announced a 22 September auction at Belfast’s Donegall Arms for Larne corn and wheat mills, Kilwaughter corn mill and Inver flour mills. It names James Holmes & Co. in possession, with separate lease interests under the heirs of the Marquis of Antrim and under the Marquis of Donegall.
This is place-study context only. The passage names no Glasgow surname and does not show that the 1669 Glasgow occurrences operated the mills or glassworks.

clusters.title: The 1653 and 1669 households
clusters.summary: A deposition and hearth-money roll record four named Glasgow/Glaskow occurrences in east Antrim.
clusters.boundary: They are separate record occurrences, not a proved founding family.

clusters.title: Hugh Glasgow of New Town, Larne
clusters.summary: The maintained church chronology identifies Hugh’s household and named children; property records also place named Glasgows in Newtown.
clusters.boundary: The surviving family chronology is derivative and does not establish Hugh’s parents or the disputed James identity.

clusters.title: James Glasgow and Sarah Murray
clusters.summary: The congregation-register chronology supports the marriage and four named children.
clusters.boundary: Their parentage is unknown; repeated names and locality do not attach them to the earlier households.

clusters.title: Robert Glasgow and Rachel Wilson
clusters.summary: Register and equity evidence reconstructs the household; the 1764 Ballykeel lease expressly names James as Robert’s son.
clusters.boundary: No inspected record proves descent from Robert Glaskow at Larne in 1653.

clusters.title: James Glasgow and Mary Crosier
clusters.summary: The maintained evidence strongly supports the couple and four named sons, including Archibald.
clusters.boundary: Their American branch does not prove the ancestry of the older Larne households.

clusters.title: James, Hugh and the 1843 bride Mary
clusters.summary: The monument documents James as elder Hugh’s son; the settlement documents a deceased Hugh’s estate connection with Mary.
clusters.boundary: No inspected record states James was the later Hugh’s father or Hugh was Mary’s father. Mary may be William’s daughter, and the 1843/1844 death-year conflict is unresolved.

clusters.title: Tennessee Robert and James J
clusters.summary: Robert’s South Carolina birth and household ages make him a worthwhile candidate for Archibald’s unaccounted-for son, and for James J’s father.
clusters.boundary: No located record names Archibald as Robert’s father or Robert as James J’s father; another age-compatible Newberry household remains a live alternative.

clusters.title: James, ropemaker, of Larne
clusters.summary: The ropemaker has a real adult and property trail; he is a candidate for an older generation in the Inishrush comparison.
clusters.boundary: No record joins him to Adam of Inishrush, and the 1762 marriage leaves Adam’s mother unresolved if this were a father–son link.

clusters.title: Adam of Inishrush
clusters.summary: Adam’s family is a meaningful collateral comparison because the ages can fit a Larne father hypothesis.
clusters.boundary: No document names Adam’s father or joins him to Larne; alternative local origins remain open.

proved: The 1764 Ballykeel lease, memorial 159661, calls James Glasgow Robert’s son.
The Larne monument names James-3991 as a son of elder Hugh-1499.
supported: Robert and Rachel’s Kilwaughter household, and James and Mary Crosier’s South Carolina continuation, are supported by concordant register, will and equity material.
hypothesis: Archibald’s missing boy may be Tennessee Robert, a possible father of James J.
The Larne ropemaker James may be Adam of Inishrush’s father.
James-3991 → Hugh-4180 → Mary-4181 is a low-confidence estate-based working chain.
unresolved: No bridge joins the 1653/1669 householders to the later Kilwaughter family.
Mary’s possible identity with William’s daughter remains conflicted by the 1843 and 1844 death evidence.

gaps.title: Inspect the Kilwaughter tenant and rental originals
gaps.why: They may name a predecessor, successor or relative across the early gap.

gaps.title: Read Hugh’s will and Mary’s property succession
gaps.why: They could distinguish the estate testator and identify the 1843 bride.

gaps.title: Inspect the 1751 and 1767 lease endorsements
gaps.why: Named lives or recitals could distinguish Hugh, William and later Larne people.

gaps.title: Read the original Kilwaughter congregation records
gaps.why: They are the test for the derivative household chronology and disputed identities.

gaps.title: Recover the Belfast captain’s will
gaps.why: It may clarify named relatives and the qualification on the 1686 date.

gaps.title: Test Archibald’s missing son and the Larne–Inishrush comparison
gaps.why: Estate, church and succession records could replace age-based hypotheses with parent statements.
